lead: Three members of the thyristor family fill gaps the SCR leaves. A TRIAC conducts in both directions and is triggered by one gate, so a single device switches AC. A DIAC is a two-terminal trigger device that breaks over at about 30 V in either direction; it gives the TRIAC a clean, symmetric gate pulse but carries no load current. A GTO (gate turn-off thyristor) is turned off by a large negative gate current, so it needs no commutation circuit. TRIACs with DIACs sit in lamp dimmers and fan regulators; GTOs drove traction before IGBTs.
prereq: You need: the SCR structure, latching and holding current, and gate triggering.

blocks.text: A TRIAC (triode AC switch) behaves like two SCRs in inverse parallel on one chip with a common gate. Its terminals are main terminal 1 (MT1), main terminal 2 (MT2) and the gate G, which sits next to MT1; all voltages are measured from MT1. When MT2 is positive, current flows MT2 → MT1; when MT2 is negative, it flows MT1 → MT2. The V–I characteristic therefore has identical blocking and conduction branches in the first and third quadrants, with breakover at ±V<sub>BO</sub>.

It is triggered in four modes, named by the sign of MT2 and of the gate, both measured from MT1: I+ (MT2 +, G +), I− (MT2 +, G −), III− (MT2 −, G −) and III+ (MT2 −, G +). Sensitivity differs: I+ is the most sensitive, I− and III− need somewhat more gate current, and III+ is the least sensitive, so most circuits use I+ and III−, or a negative gate pulse in both halves. Like an SCR, a TRIAC turns off when its current falls below the holding current near each current zero.

With an inductive load the current lags the voltage, so when the TRIAC current reaches zero the supply voltage is already large and reappears across it very fast. If this commutating dv/dt exceeds the TRIAC's rating it turns on again and the load stays on. An RC snubber across the TRIAC slows the voltage rise. Most TRIACs are made for currents up to a few tens of amperes at 50 Hz.

A DIAC is a two-terminal, bidirectional trigger diode with no gate. It blocks in both directions until the voltage across it reaches its breakover voltage V<sub>BO</sub>, typically about 30 V; its voltage then falls by several volts (a negative-resistance region) and it passes a sharp current pulse. Its V–I curve is symmetric about the origin.

In a lamp dimmer a variable resistor R and a capacitor C form a phase-shifting network across the supply. Each half-cycle the capacitor charges until its voltage reaches V<sub>BO</sub>; the DIAC fires and dumps the capacitor charge into the TRIAC gate, and the TRIAC turns on for the rest of the half-cycle. A larger R gives a later firing angle α and a dimmer lamp. Because the DIAC is symmetric, the firing angle is the same in both half-cycles, so the load sees no DC component. The control of the load voltage itself is treated under AC voltage controllers.

A GTO has the same p-n-p-n layers as an SCR, but the cathode is split into many narrow fingers surrounded by gate metal (interdigitated), and the p-n-p part has a lower gain. A positive gate pulse turns it on like an SCR. A large negative gate current pulls holes out of the P2 layer under every cathode finger, the n-p-n transistor leaves saturation, and the device turns off without any commutation circuit.

where β<sub>off</sub> is the turn-off gain (no unit), I<sub>A</sub> the anode current to be turned off and I<sub>G(off)</sub> the peak negative gate current, both in amperes. β<sub>off</sub> is only about 3 to 5.

The low turn-off gain is the GTO's price: a 600 A GTO needs a negative gate pulse of 120 A to 200 A, from a low-impedance drive. Its on-state drop is somewhat higher than an SCR's, many GTOs block little reverse voltage, and they need a turn-off snubber to limit dv/dt. GTOs were used in traction and large drives; IGBTs and IGCTs have replaced them in new designs.

examples.question: A TRIAC dimmer on a 230 V, 50 Hz supply fires at α = 90° in both half-cycles into a 100 Ω resistive lamp. Find the rms load voltage and the lamp power, using V<sub>rms</sub> = V<sub>s</sub> √(1 − α/π + sin 2α/(2π)).
steps: α = 90° = π/2 rad, so α/π = 0.5 and sin 2α = sin 180° = 0.
Check: at α = 0 the lamp would take 230² ÷ 100 = 529 W, and firing at 90° removes the first half of each half-cycle, which carries exactly half the energy of a sine wave.
examples.answer: V<sub>rms</sub> = 162.6 V and P = 264.5 W, half of the full 529 W.

examples.question: A GTO carries I<sub>A</sub> = 600 A and has a turn-off gain β<sub>off</sub> = 4. Find the peak negative gate current. If the gate current pulse is roughly a triangle of 20 µs base, drawn from a −15 V gate supply, find the gate charge, the energy taken from the gate supply per turn-off and the average gate supply power at 500 Hz.
steps: Gate charge: Q<sub>G</sub> = ½ × 150 A × 20 × 10<sup>−6</sup> s = 1.5 × 10<sup>−3</sup> C = 1.5 mC.
Energy from the 15 V supply per turn-off: E = V Q<sub>G</sub> = 15 × 1.5 × 10<sup>−3</sup> = 22.5 mJ.
Average gate supply power: P = E f = 22.5 × 10<sup>−3</sup> × 500 = 11.25 W.
examples.answer: I<sub>G(off)</sub> = 150 A, Q<sub>G</sub> = 1.5 mC, 22.5 mJ per turn-off and about 11.3 W of gate supply power, far more than an SCR gate needs.

traps: MT1 and MT2 are not anode and cathode; current flows either way. The gate and MT2 polarities are always measured from MT1.
The DIAC only triggers; the TRIAC carries the lamp current. The RC network, not the DIAC, sets the firing angle.
Writing that a TRIAC is equally sensitive in all four modes: III+ needs the most gate current.
GTO turn-off is not a small signal: with β<sub>off</sub> = 4, a 600 A GTO needs 150 A of negative gate current.
A TRIAC on an inductive load can fail to turn off because of the commutating dv/dt; the fix is a snubber, not a bigger gate pulse.

quiz.q: Name the terminals of a TRIAC and its SCR equivalent.
quiz.a: MT1, MT2 and gate; it acts like two SCRs in inverse parallel with a common gate.

quiz.q: Define the turn-off gain of a GTO.
quiz.a: β<sub>off</sub> = I<sub>A</sub> / I<sub>G(off)</sub>: the anode current to be turned off divided by the peak negative gate current needed.

quiz.q: What are the four triggering modes of a TRIAC, and which are preferred?
quiz.a: I+ (MT2 +, G +), I− (MT2 +, G −), III− (MT2 −, G −), III+ (MT2 −, G +), all measured from MT1. I+ and III− are preferred because they are the most sensitive; III+ is the least.

quiz.q: A dimmer fires at α = 90° on a 115 V supply into a 100 Ω lamp. Find the lamp power.
A GTO carries 100 A with β<sub>off</sub> = 5. Find the peak negative gate current.
Why can a TRIAC feeding a motor fail to turn off at current zero?
quiz.a: The current lags the voltage, so at current zero the supply voltage is already high and reappears across the TRIAC at a high dv/dt; junction capacitance current re-triggers it. An RC snubber that slows the voltage rise cures it.

quiz.q: Compare how an SCR and a GTO are turned off.
quiz.a: An SCR needs its anode current brought below I<sub>H</sub> by the circuit (natural or forced commutation) and reverse bias for t<sub>q</sub>; its gate cannot turn it off. A GTO turns off by a large negative gate current (I<sub>A</sub> / β<sub>off</sub>) through its interdigitated gate, with no commutation circuit, at the cost of a powerful gate drive and a turn-off snubber.

beyond: Not for the exam. TRIACs are still inside cheap lamp dimmers and fan regulators, and ‘snubberless’ TRIACs with high commutating dv/dt drive small motors and valves directly. In high power the GTO has given way to the IGCT, which turns off with a gate current equal to the whole anode current for a microsecond and needs no turn-off snubber. Search for ‘TRIAC commutating dv/dt’ and ‘IGCT versus GTO’.
